meta.title: Soufflé: private speech-to-text for macOS
meta.description: Dictate into any app, transcribe meetings that tell your voice from everyone else's, and get on-device summaries. No cloud, no accounts, no API keys.

hero.title:
Your voice never
leaves your Mac.
hero.sub: Soufflé dictates into any app, transcribes meetings that tell your voice from everyone else's, and writes the summary, all of it on-device. No cloud, no account, no API key.
hero.caption: A live meeting transcript, separating you from everyone else. No virtual audio device, nothing uploaded.

features.title: Meetings that know who is talking.
features.body: System-audio capture separates Me from Them in the live transcript, with no virtual audio device to install. Recording stays hands-off: it offers to start when a calendar meeting begins, notices when the meeting seems over, and survives a closed lid.
bullets: Optional Opus audio with a retention policy, replayable by clicking the transcript
Recovers or salvages the session if the engine stalls or the mic disappears
Everything grouped by day, with full-text search across every word

features.title: Dictate into anything, and it pastes itself back.
features.body: One global shortcut starts it from wherever you are, and the text lands in the app you were already in when you stop. Terminals and secure fields that refuse a synthetic paste can get simulated keystrokes instead.
bullets: Optional start and stop sounds, so you know the shortcut landed
A local LLM pass can polish the text before it lands, with editable prompts
French and English out of the box on the default model

features.title: The summary is written on your machine too.
features.body: Decisions, action items with owners, and the questions nobody answered, extracted alongside the summary by Apple Intelligence, or by a local Ollama when your Mac does not offer it. Transcription itself needs neither.
bullets: Editable notes and participants next to the transcript
No setup at all when Apple Intelligence is available

overlay.title: It works on top of whatever you are in.
overlay.body: Soufflé is not a window you type into. Press the shortcut and a small overlay appears above your current app. The text streams into it as you talk, a local pass tidies it up, and it lands in the field you were already using. Chat, mail, an editor, a terminal: the overlay does not care which.
bullets: The pill floats over every app and is excluded from screen recording
It grows as you talk and shrinks back when it has nothing to show
overlay.caption: Press the shortcut anywhere, talk, and the tidied text lands where your cursor already was.

models.title: Pick the trade-off you want.
models.sub: All four run locally, downloaded on first use. Switch whenever you like.

cards.name: Kyutai STT 1B
cards.desc: French and English streaming transcription, the one most people should stay on.

cards.name: Kyutai STT 2.6B
cards.desc: English only, noticeably higher quality, if you have the disk and the patience.

cards.name: Whisper Large V3 Turbo
cards.desc: Multilingual and familiar, through whisper.cpp on the GPU.

cards.name: Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3
cards.desc: 25 languages with punctuation and capitalization, fast on the CPU alone.

docs.title: Everything Soufflé does, and what it needs to do it.
docs.intro: Short pages, written for someone who has just downloaded the app. Nothing here requires an account, a key, or a network connection beyond the first model download.

blocks.p: With Homebrew:
Or download the .dmg from the latest release and drag Soufflé into Applications. Every build is signed and notarized.

table: Apple Silicon. There is no Intel build.
Dictation, meetings with your microphone only.
Meetings that capture the other participants. System-audio capture uses the Core Audio process tap, which does not exist before 14.4. On macOS 13 a meeting still records, and the app shows Mic only.
670 MB to 5.6 GB for the speech model, downloaded on first use.
Apple Intelligence, when your Mac offers it, or a local Ollama. Transcription needs neither.

blocks.p: Soufflé asks for each of these as you use the feature that needs it, never up front. Settings → Permissions shows the current state of each and links straight to the matching System Settings pane.

table: Records your voice so it can be transcribed. Needed for everything.
Captures what the other participants say, without a virtual audio device. Meetings on macOS 14.4+.
Pastes into the app you were using, and reads back your corrections when “learn from edits” is on.
Reads today's events to list them and offer to start recording. Optional.

blocks.p: A setup wizard walks through the three things that matter: picking a speech model and downloading it, granting the microphone permission, and choosing the dictation shortcut. The default shortcut is <kbd>⌘⇧Space</kbd>, and it can be rebound in Settings.

Press the shortcut anywhere, talk, press it again. The text pastes itself into whatever app had focus. Apps that reject a synthetic paste (terminals, secure fields) can receive simulated keystrokes instead; the switch is in Settings.
Optional start and stop sounds confirm the shortcut landed. Dictation polish, also optional, runs the text through a local LLM with an editable prompt template before it is pasted.

Dictation does not open a window. A small overlay, the pill, appears above whatever you are working in: a recording dot, the label, a live waveform, and a stop button. It stays 280 px wide until there is text to show, then widens to 440 px and grows line by line as you talk.

When you stop, the pill switches to Reformulating… while the local polish pass runs, then disappears as the text lands in the field you were already using. The window is excluded from screen recording, so it does not show up in the meeting you are in.
A meeting records your microphone and, on macOS 14.4+, the system audio, so the live transcript separates Me from Them as it goes.

The lifecycle is meant to be hands-off: the app offers to start when a calendar meeting begins, detects when the meeting seems over and stops on its own after warning you, pauses and resumes across lid-close and system sleep, and recovers or salvages the session if the engine stalls or the microphone disappears.
Audio recording is off by default. Turn it on and the meeting sound is kept as compact Opus files under a retention policy you set, replayable with click-to-seek from any line of the transcript.

Summaries are generated on-device, by Apple Intelligence when your Mac offers it (no setup), otherwise by a local Ollama you point the app at. Alongside the summary, Soufflé extracts decisions, action items with owners, and open questions.
Nothing about a summary is sent anywhere. If you use Ollama, the only request is to your own instance, http://localhost:11434 by default.
All models run locally and are downloaded on first use from HuggingFace. Switch at any time in Settings → Transcription.

table: Default. French + English streaming, ~2.4 GB, Metal GPU via Candle.
25 languages with punctuation and capitalization, ~670 MB int8, fast CPU inference via ONNX Runtime.

blocks.p: The privacy claim is worth checking rather than believing, so here is every outbound connection the app makes.

table: Downloads a speech model the first time you select it. Nothing is sent, and once the model is on disk transcription works offline forever.

Once a day, and whenever you press Check for updates, asks whether a newer release exists. It sends nothing but the request: no identifier, no account, no usage data. It shows a dialog and never downloads or installs anything. Turn it off in Settings → About.
Your Ollama instance, only if you enable summaries with Ollama. It is your machine unless you point it elsewhere.

blocks.p: Your audio, transcripts, notes and summaries are never sent anywhere. They live in a local SQLite database, and Settings → Data exports or deletes the lot.
Any meeting exports as Markdown, JSON, or SRT/VTT subtitles. The whole archive exports as a plain folder of Markdown and JSON. No proprietary container, nothing to migrate out of later.

The bundled souffle-mcp sidecar lets Claude Desktop, Claude Code or any MCP client search and read your transcripts. It is read-only, fully local, and works even when the app is closed. Ready-made configuration snippets live in Settings → Data.
The souffle binary transcribes a file without launching the app. It ships inside the app bundle and is not added to your PATH, so invoke it by full path or symlink it once.

blocks.code:
# Run directly
"/Applications/Soufflé.app/Contents/MacOS/souffle" --list-engines

# Or expose it as a `souffle` command
ln -s "/Applications/Soufflé.app/Contents/MacOS/souffle" /usr/local/bin/souffle

# Transcribe a file, JSON on stdout
souffle --transcribe-file audio.wav --json

blocks.p: --repeat N runs the same file N times, which doubles as a benchmark harness for comparing models on your machine.
Requires an Apple Silicon Mac, Rust, Node.js 18+, and cmake (brew install cmake).

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/damione1/souffle.git
cd souffle
npm install
npm run tauri dev

blocks.p: Soufflé is early and actively developed. Every release is signed and notarized and the engineering is covered by a large test suite, but the app has been run on very few machines, and the fragile parts are the ones that vary most from one Mac to another: audio routing, Bluetooth headsets, docks, and permission prompts.
If something breaks there, open an issue with your macOS version, your Mac model, and the audio devices involved.
